findings.title: MCP tool outputs are unbounded - no truncation or size caps on any of the 6 tool results
findings.description: buff_expand embeds the FULL generated Rust source in the tool text (tools.rs:638-642); buff_check returns every diagnostic uncapped (399-428); buff_complete serializes the entire CompletionResponse (510-525); buff_format returns full source (596-600). Grep for truncat/max/cap/limit in buff-mcp/src returns zero matches. Large .buff inputs funnel megabytes into agent context windows. Verified: no outbound LLM calls, no API keys, stdio-only, tools-only capabilities (no sampling).
findings.root_cause: T62 shipped a thin delegation layer (every handler returns ToolResult::ok(text) verbatim) with no output-budget policy; cost hygiene was out of the task spec.
findings.impact: AI agents consuming buff-mcp can burn unbounded context tokens per tools/call on big files or error-heavy projects; repeated buff_check loops on a large project multiply cost. No repo-side API bill (server is local), so severity stays low.
findings.recommendation: Add a shared output budget in ToolResult (e.g. 64 KiB): over-cap results get head+tail slices, byte counts, and an elision note pointing at the equivalent CLI command for full output.
findings.fix_guide: 1. Add MAX_TOOL_OUTPUT const + elide() helper in tools.rs (or ToolResult::ok). 2. Route all six handle_* success paths through it. 3. Append an explicit [truncated: N of M bytes] note (agents reason better with explicit elision). 4. Unit test with a >64KiB fixture asserting the elision marker appears. 5. Note the budget in crates/buff-mcp/AGENTS.md MCP TOOLS table.

effort_estimate.breakdown: helper+const 15m; rewire 6 handlers 15m; unit test 15m; AGENTS.md note 15m

detection_method.query: (?i)(truncat|max_?bytes|MAX_OUTPUT|char_limit|cap_) over crates/buff-mcp/src -> 0 hits; manual read of tools.rs handlers

confidence.rationale: Full read of all six handlers confirms zero truncation logic; only uncertainty is whether a cap lives in buff-lsp handlers (delegated outputs return verbatim LSP shapes).

findings.title: Toolchain and checkout actions use mutable major-tag refs while all sibling actions are SHA-pinned; AGENTS.md still claims CI uses unpinned @master
findings.description: ci.yml (7 occurrences: lines 65, 97, 128, 150, 165, 280, 318) and security.yml (lines 23, 54) reference dtolnay/rust-toolchain@v1 and actions/checkout@v4 (also 11 occurrences) - mutable major tags that can be retargeted upstream. Every OTHER third-party action in these workflows IS commit-SHA-pinned with a version comment: EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@3c63498..., Swatinem/rust-cache@e18b49..., docker/setup-buildx@8d2750c..., docker/build-push-action@ca052bb..., actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8..., softprops/action-gh-release@3bb1273.... Additionally AGENTS.md line 229 asserts '.github/workflows/ci.yml uses dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master' - stale; the actual ref is @v1, and rust-toolchain.toml/CI both agree on toolchain: 1.95.0, so the documented 'toolchain mismatch' risk is misdescribed while the real (smaller) mutable-ref exposure goes undocumented.
findings.root_cause: A hardening pass SHA-pinned the newer/less-common actions but left the two most common ones (checkout, rust-toolchain) on mutable tags; AGENTS.md was written against an older @master state and not updated after the move to @v1.
findings.impact: A upstream tag retarget or compromise of dtolnay/rust-toolchain or actions/checkout injects arbitrary code into every CI job that installs the toolchain - the highest-privilege step in the pipeline. Inconsistent pinning also undermines the audit trail the SHA-pinned actions were pinned for. The stale AGENTS.md note means contributors auditing supply-chain will look for a risk that no longer exists and miss the one that does.
findings.recommendation: Pin dtolnay/rust-toolchain and actions/checkout to full commit SHAs with '# v1' / '# v4' comments matching the existing house style (or adopt Dependabot/renovate with 'pin GitHub Actions' to maintain SHAs automatically). Then update AGENTS.md NOTES line 229 to state the @v1 + SHA-pin arrangement and drop the obsolete @master mismatch paragraph.

- uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@v1
  with:
    toolchain: 1.95.0
    components: rustfmt
fix_examples.after:
- uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4
- uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain<sha-of-v1-tip> # v1
  with:
    toolchain: 1.95.0
    components: rustfmt

findings.fix_guide: 1) Resolve current SHAs: git ls-remote https://github.com/actions/checkout v4 and git ls-remote https://github.com/dtolnay/rust-toolchain v1 (or take them from the workflow run logs' 'Download action repository' lines). 2) Replace @v4/@v1 with @<sha> plus trailing '# v4'/'# v1' comments in ci.yml (11 + 7 spots) and security.yml (2 + 2 spots); release.yml/pages.yml/docker.yml if they use the same actions. 3) Update AGENTS.md line 229 to describe the SHA-pinned setup and delete the @master claim. 4) Optionally add .github/dependabot.yml with package-ecosystem 'github-actions' + allow 'pinned' to keep SHAs fresh.

effort_estimate.breakdown: SHA resolution 10m; edit 4 workflow files 15m; AGENTS.md update 5m; verify one CI run 10m

detection_method.query: Select-String -Path .github\workflows\*.yml -Pattern 'uses: .*@'; compare SHA-pinned vs tag-pinned refs

references: C:\Users\vsbb1\source\repos\buff\.github\workflows\ci.yml lines 53-68 (contrast SHA-pinned cargo-deny-action line 54 vs checkout@v4 line 53/rust-toolchain@v1 line 65)

confidence.rationale: All refs enumerated directly from the workflow files; the inconsistency is mechanically verifiable. Severity held at medium because the toolchain VERSION itself is consistently 1.95.0 everywhere (no version drift), so exposure is limited to action-code supply chain, not toolchain-version surprises.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: The audit brief framed this as '@master unpinned major' - reality is @v1, which is still a mutable ref; either way the internal inconsistency against the repo's own SHA-pinning house style is objective, and the AGENTS.md staleness is quoted verbatim. No project convention endorses mutable tags for the already-SHA-pinned siblings.

findings.title: AGENTS.md dioxus caret-pin drift warning is obsolete: workspace uses exact =0.7.9 pins since T29, and no CI re-test guard exists or is needed
findings.description: AGENTS.md line 236 warns 'dioxus = "0.7" and dioxus-ssr = "0.7" are workspace caret pins... re-test on every minor bump'. Reality (root Cargo.toml lines 540-563): T29 (v1.25 tech-debt batch) upgraded both to EXACT pins dioxus = "=0.7.9" and dioxus-ssr = "=0.7.9" specifically 'to prevent surprise breakage from dioxus-rsx proc-macro changes'. The companion question from the audit scope ('is the re-test guard documented in CI?'): no dioxus-specific job exists in ci.yml; dioxus breakage would surface only via the clippy hard gate (compile-time) and the advisory continue-on-error test jobs.
findings.root_cause: T29 changed the pins but the AGENTS.md NOTES section (which the same T29-era edits touched elsewhere) kept the older caret-pin text.
findings.impact: Low: documentation overstates a risk that has been mitigated. findings.recommendation: Rewrite AGENTS.md line 236 to: (a) state the exact =0.7.9 pins and their T29 rationale; (b) re-point the re-test obligation at MANUAL bumps - 'when bumping the =0.7.9 pins, run buff-ui-dioxus + ssr tests and the wasm build, since dioxus-rsx internals are not semver-covered'; (c) optionally note that ci.yml clippy is the only hard gate covering dioxus compile breakage.

findings.title: DAP backend debuggee child process leaks on every error path (no Drop/kill guard)
findings.description: run_session spawns lldb-dap (BackendProcess holding std::process::Child) then translates/forwards editor messages. Six bail-out points use `?` (read L241, decode L248, translate L250, encode L251, stdin write/flush L255/L258): any of them returns Err WITHOUT kill()/wait() on backend.child and without joining the backend reader thread. Only the clean stdin-EOF path (L242-245) reaches the drain logic at L264-285. backend.rs:137 comment says the child is 'kept for kill on drop' but no `impl Drop` exists anywhere in buff-dap/src (verified by grep).
findings.root_cause: Cleanup was written as straight-line code after the loop instead of an RAII guard; `?` short-circuits skip it. The 'kill on drop' Drop impl was never implemented despite the comment.
findings.impact: Any protocol error, malformed editor message, or I/O hiccup leaves an orphaned lldb-dap/debuggee process (and a blocked reader thread) per failed session; repeated debug-session failures accumulate zombie processes on the user's machine.
findings.recommendation: Add a session guard struct (or impl Drop for BackendProcess) that kills + waits the child on drop, and use it for all early-return paths; join/abort the reader thread via the guard too.
fix_guide: Wrap backend.child in a Drop guard struct at spawn time in backend.rs
Replace the manual drop(stdin)+wait() sequence with normal scope exit
On the clean path, take the child out of the guard (mem::take) before the existing wait() for the exit-status check
Add an integration test that forces a decode error and asserts no child survives

effort_estimate.breakdown: 30m guard struct + spawn rewiring, 30m clean-path mem::take refactor, 30m leak test

confidence.rationale: Code-path reading confirms 6 `?` exits before any kill/wait; grep proves no Drop impl; only normal-EOF path cleans up

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: No allowlist or AGENTS.md entry documents skipping child cleanup; the backend.rs comment itself promises kill-on-drop, making this an unimplemented intention, not a choice

findings.title: SQLite storage performs blocking file I/O directly inside async axum handlers (no spawn_blocking)
findings.description: With BUFF_REGISTRY_DB_PATH set (durable mode, T57), all 22 storage call sites in handlers.rs (publish put_version L447, get_tarball L515, list_versions L545, validate_token L356, ...) execute synchronous rusqlite queries + blob writes while holding the connection Mutex directly on tokio worker threads. Zero occurrences of spawn_blocking in the crate (verified). The registry AGENTS.md explicitly anticipated this: 'A real DB-backed impl can wrap its async ops in tokio::task::spawn_blocking' - the shipped SqliteStorage did not apply that mitigation.
findings.root_cause: Sync Storage trait called from async handlers; SQLite backend added in T57 without the documented spawn_blocking wrapper, so disk-latency queries park tokio workers.
findings.impact: Slow disk or a large tarball publish stalls a tokio worker; concurrent requests queue behind the connection Mutex held for full I/O duration (not the documented nanosecond in-memory case), degrading or stalling the registry under load.
findings.recommendation: Wrap SqliteStorage call sites in tokio::task::spawn_blocking (per-crate AGENTS.md already prescribes the pattern), or make handlers call through a spawn_blocking adapter on AppState when the backend is SQLite.

fix_guide: Add a spawn_blocking helper on AppState used by all handler storage calls
Keep InMemoryStorage on the fast path (skip spawn_blocking for it or accept the tiny cost)
Add a test with a large tarball asserting other requests proceed concurrently

effort_estimate.breakdown: 60m adapter + 22 call sites, 45m error plumbing (JoinError), 45m concurrency test

confidence.rationale: 22 sync call sites verified in async handlers; spawn_blocking absent; only uncertainty is practical latency impact (rusqlite is fast for this dataset)

findings.title: Registry server lacks graceful shutdown (axum::serve without with_graceful_shutdown)

findings.title: Kernelspec advertises interrupt_mode='signal' but the kernel has no SIGINT handler - interrupt kills the kernel
findings.description: KERNEL_INTERRUPT_MODE = "signal" (kernelspec.rs:50) tells Jupyter to interrupt via SIGINT (Unix) / CTRL_BREAK_EVENT (Windows). The Rust kernel process installs no signal handler (grep 'interrupt|SIGINT' in buff-jupyter/src: only the ACK-only interrupt_request at kernel.rs:250-255, documented as 'ack only, cancellation lands in T129c+'). With the OS default disposition, that signal terminates the whole kernel process - so 'Interrupt kernel' in Jupyter kills the session (losing all cross-cell state) rather than stopping the running cell.
findings.root_cause: T129a shipped ACK-only interrupts and chose the default 'signal' mode without either honoring signals or declaring 'message' mode; the documented limitation covers interrupt_request handling but not the kernel-death consequence of signal mode.
findings.impact: Users interrupting a long cell lose the entire session state; on Windows, CTRL_BREAK_EVENT emulation may also hard-exit. Documented gap understates the blast radius.
findings.recommendation: Short term: install a SIGINT handler that sets a cancellation flag checked between eval steps (or between rustc-spawn phases); alternatively document 'Interrupt kernel terminates this kernel in v1.7' in lib.rs and kernelspec docs until T129c lands.

Check the flag between eval/rustc phases and emit an 'interrupted' error status
Document the interim behavior in kernel.rs module docs

findings.title: Byte-offset-to-line/col lookup reimplemented in 5 crates despite canonical buff-lang-error::SourceFile
findings.description: The line-start-table + binary-search byte-offset-to-(line,col) algorithm exists in SIX independent implementations: (1) canonical crates\buff-lang-error\src\source_map.rs:67-75 compute_line_starts + :45-63 SourceFile::lookup (char-counted columns); (2) crates\buff-lang-pipeline\src\error_mapper.rs:431-449 private byte_line_starts + byte_offset_to_line_col; (3) crates\buff-dap\src\translation.rs:276 compute_line_starts + :290 line_start_offset (reverse direction); (4) crates\buff-lang-cli\src\commands\coverage.rs:287 line_starts; (5) crates\buff-lang-cli\src\commands\refactor.rs:502-523 private LineTable struct; (6) crates\buff-lsp\src\position.rs:36-93 (EXCLUDED from the finding â€” self-documented in-module as the deliberate LSP-specific counterpart). buff-lang-error is the leaf crate every workspace member already depends on, and SourceFile::new/lookup are public; duplicates 2-5 could construct a SourceFile and delegate. Column semantics have already drifted between copies (char-counted in error crate, byte-based in error_mapper, line-only in LineTable), which is the classic divergence cost of copy-paste infrastructure.
findings.root_cause: Tooling crates (error_mapper, dap, coverage, refactor) were each built in separate T-numbered tasks; each task re-solved the offset-to-line problem locally instead of extending the leaf crate. buff-lang-error does not expose a path-parameter-free constructor or a public line-to-offset (reverse) API, which made reuse marginally inconvenient and invited reimplementation.
findings.impact: Five maintenance surfaces for one algorithm; future fixes (e.g. CRLF handling, UTF-16 columns for LSP parity, O(log n) reverse lookup) must be applied five times or the tools silently diverge in reported line/col numbers for the same .buff source. Diagnostic line numbers are user-facing â€” divergence between buff check, buff coverage and buff refactor output erodes trust.
findings.recommendation: Consolidate on buff-lang-error::SourceFile: (a) add a path-optional constructor (SourceFile::from_str(content) with empty path) and a public line_start_offset(line) reverse method for buff-dap; (b) replace error_mapper.rs byte_line_starts/byte_offset_to_line_col, translation.rs compute_line_starts/line_start_offset, coverage.rs line_starts, and refactor.rs LineTable with SourceFile construction + lookup calls; (c) leave buff-lsp position.rs as-is (documented deliberate counterpart) but note in its doc comment which semantics differ.
findings.fix_guide: 1) In buff-lang-error/src/source_map.rs add `pub fn from_content(content: String) -> Self` (path: PathBuf::new()) and `pub fn line_start_offset(&self, line: usize) -> Option<usize>` (inverse of lookup via line_starts index). 2) Keep the existing SourceFile::lookup signature â€” it is the byteâ†’(line,col) primitive both directions need. 3) Migrate one consumer per commit with its tests green (error_mapper â†’ coverage â†’ refactor â†’ dap), keeping behavior byte-identical: note error_mapper counted BYTE columns while SourceFile::lookup counts CHAR columns â€” for ASCII sources identical; verify the buffhtml fixtures still pass, and if byte-column behavior is load-bearing, add a byte_col variant rather than silently changing output. 4) Do NOT touch buff-lsp/src/position.rs (documented LSP-specific counterpart per its module doc). 5) Add a line to buff-lang-error/AGENTS.md declaring SourceFile the single text-position primitive.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 20 min SourceFile API additions + 40 min four consumer migrations + 20 min test verification incl. column-semantics check + 10 min AGENTS.md note

confidence.rationale: All six sites verified by direct read or line-precise grep; the four undocumented duplicates are plain-code identical algorithms. Only residual uncertainty is whether byte-vs-char column semantics are load-bearing for some consumer, which affects the migration recipe, not the existence of the duplication.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: Four of five duplicate sites carry no documentation claiming deliberateness; the one documented counterpart (buff-lsp position.rs) was explicitly excluded. buff-lang-error AGENTS.md says 'Don't introduce a competing location type' â€” the private duplicates contradict that spirit.

findings.title: Pedantic-tier modernization debt is unmeasured and un-gated; verified instances in buff-lang-error (leaf crate)

(clippy::format_push_string â€” extra allocation per rendered diagnostic), and :606 source[..start].rfind('\n').map(|i| i + 1).unwrap_or(0) (clippy::map_unwrap_or; sibling :609-612 has the same shape for line_end). findings.title: Jupyter kernel HMAC verification is a no-op stub; all inbound messages accepted
findings.description: verify_message() returns Ok(()) unconditionally: after the key-empty early return it computes frames_for_signing() then discards them with 'let _ = frames;' and returns Ok(()) without ever calling hmac::verify. The on-wire hmac_hex frame is discarded by parse_message() (lines 271-312) so it is not even available. The working verifier verify_message_with_signature() is marked #[allow(dead_code)] (line 338) and never invoked. Main loop line 225 calls the stub, so unsigned/forged execute_request messages are compiled and executed (rustc spawn + binary execution), violating the Jupyter spec requirement that unverified messages be dropped.
findings.root_cause: parse_message() drops the signature frame and verify_message() was left as an unimplemented stub; the correct verifier exists but was never wired into the dispatch loop.
findings.impact: Any local process can send execute_request to the kernel's shell socket and run arbitrary Buff code (full rustc compile + native execution) without the shared key. If the kernel is bound non-loopback (see AUD-SEC-002) this becomes unauthenticated remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: Retain hmac_hex in WireMessage, call hmac::verify(key, frames, sig) in verify_message for every shell and control message, remove #[allow(dead_code)] from verify_message_with_signature, and add an integration test asserting unsigned messages are dropped when a key is configured.
fix_guide: Add signature_hex field to WireMessage; capture post[1] (hmac frame index) in parse_message instead of discarding it.
Change verify_message to take the signature and delegate to hmac::verify; call it for both shell and control dispatch paths.
Delete the #[allow(dead_code)] variant or make it the single implementation; add a test that a message with wrong signature is dropped when key is non-empty.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 60 min wire-format change + 30 min loop wiring + 30 min tests

findings.technology: Rust, zeromq, hmac-sha256, Jupyter kernel protocol v5

findings.title: Kernel binds sockets to arbitrary connection-file IP; no loopback restriction or warning

findings.title: buffup verifies downloads with checksum from the same origin as the artifact (no signature)
findings.description: fetch_checksum_sidecar() downloads '<tarball_url>.sha256' from the same GitHub host serving the tarball (line 122: format!("{tarball_url}.sha256")); install.rs:78-84 compares SHA-256. This defends against corruption only: any adversary able to substitute the tarball (compromised release workflow, GitHub account, malicious redirect of both URLs) can equally substitute the sidecar. The installed artifact is an executable placed on PATH, so the trust requirement is integrity against an active adversary, which requires an independent signing key (rustup uses GPG; Homebrew uses its own seal). --skip-checksum is documented and warned, so the flag itself is not a finding.
findings.root_cause: P0.9 hardening added integrity verification but no out-of-band trust anchor; sidecar trust equals artifact trust by construction.
findings.impact: A supply-chain compromise of the release channel defeats the only download-integrity control; users executing `buffup install` would run attacker-controlled binaries with the checksum reporting OK.
findings.recommendation: Publish a detached minisign/sigstore signature made by a long-lived key whose public half ships in buffup (or is pinned via a separate channel); verify the signature (not just the hash) before unpack; keep the sha256 check as a fast-fail.
fix_guide: Add release workflow step producing a minisign/sigstore signature over the tarball.
Embed the verifying public key in the buffup binary; fetch and verify signature before extract.
Document the trust model in crates/buffup/README.md.

effort_estimate.breakdown: 120 min workflow + 90 min verify impl + 60 min tests/docs; workflow changes need release-infra coordination

findings.technology: Rust, reqwest (rustls), sha2, minisign/sigstore, GitHub Releases

confidence.rationale: Code path read directly; the weakness is architectural (same-origin sidecar) and certain, but severity is medium because exploitation requires compromising the HTTPS/GitHub release channel.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: The check exists and is commented as a supply-chain mitigation (install.rs:69-70); the finding is that the mitigation's trust anchor is circular, not that code is missing.

findings.title: Registry bearer and session tokens stored unhashed at rest in SQLite
findings.description: add_token() inserts the raw bearer token ('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tokens (token) VALUES (?1)', line 211) and session creation stores raw session tokens in the sessions table (line 572). validate_token() then compares by SQL string equality (lines 396-408); InMemoryStorage uses HashSet::contains (storage.rs:587-593). Any read of registry.db (backup leak, path traversal elsewhere, incident response artifact) yields live publish credentials. crates.io stores only SHA-256 digests of tokens for exactly this reason. The non-constant-time comparison is low practical risk (network timing over SQL/B-tree and Rust's SipHash seeding) and is noted, not the core issue.

findings.title: buff login writes ~/.buff/credentials without restrictive permissions
findings.description: save_credentials_to() creates parent dirs and writes the TOML containing the bearer token with plain fs::write (line 238). On Unix with default umask 022 the file lands 0644, readable by every local user on shared/CI hosts; no 0600 chmod (Unix) or restrictive ACL (Windows) is applied, unlike `cargo login` which sets 0600. The doc comment only acknowledges missing atomic write ('temp-file + rename' future hardening, line 224) and is silent on permissions, so this is not a documented acceptance.
findings.root_cause: Plain fs::write used for a secret-bearing file without post-write permission tightening.
findings.impact: On multi-user Unix systems any local account can read the registry token and publish packages impersonating the victim.
findings.recommendation: After write, set mode 0600 on Unix via std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt (and pre-create with OpenOptions mode 0o600); on Windows note that profile-dir ACLs apply, or set an owner-only ACL; write via temp file + rename for atomicity at the same time.

fix_guide: Apply 0600 via PermissionsExt on unix after write (cfg-gated).

findings.title: Jupyter kernel protocol core (kernel.rs run loop + execution.rs) never driven by any test
findings.description: kernel.rs is the largest file in buff-jupyter (1,470 lines, 64KB) and exposes the entire kernel as `Kernel::new(transport, conn)` + `pub async fn run()` - the Jupyter message loop handling execute_request/execute_reply/iopub. The crate's 5 test files (connection_tests, hmac_tests, kernelspec_tests, kernel_info_tests, wire_tests; ~17KB total vs 175KB of src) import only the peripheral helpers: connection::ConnectionFile, hmac::{sign,verify}, kernelspec, messages::{KernelInfoReply, BANNER}, wire::{MessageHeader, WireMessage}. No test imports kernel::Kernel, calls run(), or performs an execute_request -> execute_reply/status=iopub round-trip. execution.rs (10.5KB, cross-cell state) is likewise unreferenced. kernel.rs contains no inline #[cfg(test)] module either.
findings.root_cause: T129 testing focused on the wire-protocol building blocks (HMAC signing, header serialization, connection-file parsing) because they are pure and trivially testable; the stateful kernel loop needs a mock transport + in-memory ZMQ substitute that was deferred and never revisited.
findings.impact: The single most user-visible behavior of the Jupyter integration - 'run this cell, get output, keep session state' - has zero regression protection. A protocol bug (wrong reply status, dropped iopub stream message, broken cross-cell state) would ship undetected and only appear as a broken kernel in real notebooks.
findings.recommendation: Add crates/buff-jupyter/tests/kernel_roundtrip.rs with a mock Transport impl (the Kernel is generic over T) feeding a scripted sequence: kernel_info_request, execute_request x2 (second referencing the first's binding), shutdown_request; assert reply msg_type/status/iopub ordering and cross-cell state survival. This requires no ZMQ - the generic transport boundary already exists.
findings.fix_guide: 1) Confirm the generic bound on Kernel::new (transport trait) in kernel.rs. 2) Implement a MockTransport over Vec<Vec<u8>> frames. 3) Script kernel_info + execute x2 + shutdown; drive the loop for N messages instead of forever (may need a small run-for-N test seam). 4) Assert msg_type sequence, reply status, iopub stream frames, and cross-cell state. 5) `cargo test -p buff-jupyter --test kernel_roundtrip`.

effort_estimate.human_readable: ~1 day (mock transport + loop seam + assertions; largest single item in this audit)
